steps.title: Your country is a small part of the world
steps.body: All companies on stock exchanges make up the world market. Germany is about 2% of it. Japan is about 5%. A big economy can still be a small part. Many people invest mostly in their own country. This is called [[home-bias]]. Investing across many countries is called [[diversification]]. A world fund holds prices in dollars, yen and pounds, so exchange rates move its value in euros too. That is [[currency-risk]]. The numbers are rounded.

stat.label: Germany's share of the world stock market

steps.prompt: A bad year: one country falls 40%, the rest of the world 10%. Find a mix where the total loss is 15% or less.

worldMove.label: Change in the rest of the world

goal.hint: Try putting less money in the one country.

steps.note: This is an example. In a real crisis, all countries can fall at the same time.

steps.prompt: Look at the chart. What does it show?
options: The more money is in the falling country, the bigger the total loss
Spreading the money makes the loss bigger
It does not matter how much money is in one country
steps.explanation: With 0% in that country, the total loss is 10%. With 100%, it is 40%. Each extra share in that country makes the total loss bigger.

chart.caption: Total change of the money. That country falls 40%, the rest of the world falls 10%.

steps.prompt: The euro becomes 20% stronger against the dollar. A dollar fund's price stays the same. What happens to its value in euros?
options: Nothing, because the fund's price did not change
steps.explanation: Each dollar now buys fewer euros, so the fund is worth less in euros. This is [[currency-risk]]. It can help you or hurt you.

steps.prompt: True or false: a fund that invests all over the world cannot lose value in a bad year.
steps.explanation: False. In a bad year, most countries fall at the same time. A spread fund usually loses less than its worst country, but it still loses.

steps.title: How spread your money is
steps.body: **{worldShare}** of your investment account is in funds that invest all over the world. **{europeShare}** is in funds that invest only in Europe. If Europe has a bad year, that part loses the most.

stat.label: of your investments spread across the world

steps.prompt: Imagine Europe falls 40% and the rest of the world 10%. This is what it does to your account.

worldMove.label: Change in the rest of the world

goal.hint: Move a slider to see the result change.

steps.note: The first slider starts at your real share. This is an example, not a forecast.

steps.title: Your decision
steps.body: **{europeShare}** of your investment account depends on Europe only. What is the most you want to have in one country or region? You choose the limit.

scenes.desc: Each country is a small part of the world stock market. Investing mostly in your own country is called [[home-bias]]. Spreading money across many countries is called [[diversification]]. The numbers are rounded.

Germany is about 2% of it. Japan is about 5%.
